cues.text:
The pilot is complete and the scorecard
starts with two counts.

Forty eligible requests in the baseline
and forty in the pilot.

Each row is one pull request, even if
three teammates reviewed it.

Count the rows and confirm the same
eligibility rule applied in both
windows.

In this synthetic sample every request
merged and had the same defect
follow-up.

In your own data, flag rows with missing
dates or insufficient follow-up.

That tells the next reader which
denominator you used for each metric.

Read the wait row first. Eighteen minus
thirteen is five fewer business hours
before the first human review.

Thirteen is within the fourteen-hour
target. Next read the effort row.

Twenty-six minus twenty-four gives us a
two-minute increase in median active
review.

Twenty-six fits the twenty-seven minute
limit. Say both findings in the same
meeting.

This result can reflect a shorter queue
alongside a little more reviewer work.

Report the medians separately because
they describe different parts of the
review process.

Ask which row would reveal a reviewer
workload problem.

Now divide the rework count by the
number of eligible requests.

In the baseline, six divided by forty
gives fifteen percent.

In the pilot, seven divided by forty
gives seventeen and a half percent.

That is two and a half percentage points
above the limit,

even though the count changed by just
one.

This is the guardrail the team missed.
The defect count is one in each group,
or two and a half percent.

With one event in each, report the
counts and be careful about drawing a
trend.
Open the pilot ledger.

Charge a hundred dollars for allocated
licenses,

twenty for approved remote test and
review workspace use,
and a hundred and twenty for enablement.

A hundred plus twenty plus a hundred and
twenty gives two hundred and forty.

Divide by forty eligible requests and
you get six dollars per request.

The cap was three hundred, leaving sixty
dollars of headroom.

The ledger tracks these incremental
expenses. Reviewer minutes appear on the
effort row.

If the organization plans to value that
labor,
agree on the rate and allocation first.

A scorecard tells us which question to
ask next.

Open the seven rework cases and read the
file lists and review reasons.

In four cases the reviewer asked the
author to remove edits outside the
ticket.

For instance, a one-line validator fix
also reformatted a configuration file.

Separate that extra change and note why
the reviewer asked for it.

Four of seven is enough to make scope
worth investigating here.

It gives the team something concrete to
improve.

Share the pattern and example. Keep
individual usage statistics out of that
discussion.

Prepare a short update for the decision
meeting.

The median wait reached thirteen hours,
the median active review stayed within

its limit, and spending stayed within
budget.

Rework missed the threshold. Add the
sample size, the seven rework cases,
and any reason the windows might differ.

For example, a change in reviewer
coverage could affect wait time.

Here's the exercise. Try reporting the
results in two sentences with one

benefit, one guardrail miss, and no
causal claim.

A decision owner should be able to tell
exactly what needs attention.
